thesis: Hormozi models trust through vulnerability, reliability, incentives, and whether disclosed information is later used to harm.
summary: Hormozi proposes a behavioral account of trust based on who is exposed to harm and whether harm comes from another person or consequences of failed action or advice. He recommends looking at a person's record and incentives before disclosing something material. The relational benefit is greater shared context, which can enable better help. Trustworthiness then requires both a safe immediate response and not weaponizing the disclosure later. He separately emphasizes keeping commitments and giving reliable advice. The model is his conceptual framework, illustrated with hypothetical family examples and a planned company disclosure, not a validated psychology taxonomy.

insights.title: Trust exposes something valued to possible harm
insights.explanation: The model treats disclosure, delegated responsibility, and following advice as different ways of becoming vulnerable. It should not be mistaken for an exhaustive definition of human trust.
insights.quote: if I trust someone it means that I make myself punishable by them
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: Evaluate both behavior and incentives
insights.explanation: The proposed filter asks whether the person previously protected confidences and whether betrayal is attractive to them. Good incentives alone are not supplied as sufficient proof.
insights.quote: do they have a track record of protecting what they've been given
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: More context can improve the help a relationship permits
insights.explanation: The benefit of disclosure is not vulnerability for its own sake. The speaker argues that knowing more about another person can make assistance more relevant.
insights.quote: there's a limit to how much I can help someone if I don't know anything about them
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: Do not weaponize a confidence later
insights.explanation: A warm initial response is only part of trustworthiness. The framework also excludes later use in arguments or sharing it with someone else who causes harm.
insights.quote: the second thing is that it doesn't get used in the future against them
insights.speaker: unresolved

insights.title: Distinguish safe confidences from reliable action and advice
insights.explanation: Keeping a promise and giving useful advice build a different kind of confidence from not exploiting secrets. The transcript distinguishes these mechanisms rather than treating trust as one undifferentiated trait.
insights.quote: If you say "I'm going to pick up the kid," and then you do the likelihood that they'll trust you pick up the kid in the future goes up
insights.speaker: unresolved

review_status: Codex editorial draft; complete local transcript read; claims not independently verified
synthesis_method: Direct Codex extraction from complete local transcript; exact quotations verified locally
context_and_limits: The four-type model and the claim that one betrayal can end trust are the speaker's generalizations. His wife/mother example is explicitly made up. The company presentation is planned for the next day, not a completed trust-building outcome. Strategic vulnerability does not establish that all disclosure is prudent.
review_changes: Adds the two-axis model, confidentiality versus competence distinction, delayed misuse risk, and hypothetical/planned status of the examples.
